title: Payments slow right after release
executive_summary:
INC-005 (SEV1): Payment and order latency and errors degraded from about 11:40Z on 2026-09-14, shortly after the payment-service 5.8.0 release was reported. The investigation status is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED. The leading hypothesis (H1, confidence 0.9) is storage degradation on the postgres volume vol-0a3f, which slowed writes and checkpoints, held database connections, and caused statement timeouts on charges.insert (payment) and orders.update (order). The earliest anomaly is the vol-0a3f write-latency WARN at 11:21:06Z (logpat-postgres-d629c24d), followed by disk_io_wait rising from a 2.0 ms baseline to a 107 ms window mean from 11:22Z (met-postgres-disk_io_wait_ms-1110-1205), postgres p95 latency rising from 12 ms to a 668 ms mean from 11:23Z (met-postgres-p95_latency_ms-1110-1205), and slow checkpoints and WAL writes from 11:24Z (logpat-postgres-7ce84fae). Connection utilisation rose from 40% to 74% mean from 11:26Z. Statement timeouts appeared in order-service from 11:28:12Z and payment-service from 11:28:17Z. Payment error rate rose to a window mean of 8.8% from 11:30Z (met-payment-service-error_rate-1130-1200).

The 5.8.0 release was not the cause. H2 (deployment regression) is rejected: the first timeouts precede the 11:32Z deployment, payment p99 is flat through the release, and the postgres degradation predates it (dep-31448d11, logpat-payment-service-e14637d4). H3 (report_rollup() saturation) is rejected as the root cause because report_rollup() started at 11:28:01Z, after the storage anomalies began; it may have aggravated contention but its impact is not quantified.

critic_review.summary: H1 (storage degradation on postgres volume vol-0a3f) is the leading hypothesis and is well supported in time. The earliest anomaly is the vol-0a3f write-latency WARN at 11:21:06Z, followed by disk_io_wait onset at 11:22Z, p95 onset at 11:23Z, slow WAL/checkpoints from 11:24Z, connection utilisation onset at 11:26Z, and statement timeouts in payment and order services from 11:28Z. Independent sources (postgres logs, disk metrics, latency metrics, connection metrics, app logs) agree on this sequence. H2 is rejected: the first charges.insert timeout (11:28:17Z) and the order-service timeouts (11:28:12Z) both precede the 5.8.0 startup at 11:32Z, payment p99 is flat through the release, and the postgres degradation predates the release. H3 is rejected as the root cause: report_rollup() started at 11:28:01Z, after the storage and checkpoint anomalies began. It may be an aggravating load factor on an already degraded volume, but it does not explain the onset. The pre-check blockers on H2 and H3 are valid.

assessments.reasoning: Storage write-latency WARN (11:21:06Z) precedes disk IO wait (11:22Z), p95 (11:23Z), checkpoint slowdown (11:24Z), connection saturation (11:26Z), and app timeouts (11:28Z). Consistent multi-source chain. CPU not saturated, which fits an I/O bottleneck. Storage-layer events and pg_stat wait events are not available to the team's tools, but that does not block approval of the category and culprit.

Timeouts start at 11:28 (payment) and 11:28:12 (order-service, not deployed) before the 11:32 release. Payment p99 shows no change. Storage degradation at 11:21 precedes the release. Timing contradicts causation.

report_rollup() began at 11:28:01Z, after disk IO wait (11:22Z), checkpoint slowdown (11:24Z), and connection climb (11:26Z) were already underway. It can only be a contributing load on top of the storage fault, not the root cause. Pre-check blocker confirmed.

root_cause_statement: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence): infrastructure_degradation in postgres - Storage degradation on postgres volume vol-0a3f slowed writes and checkpoints, holding DB connections and causing payment charges.insert and order orders.update statement timeouts.
corrective_actions: Investigate and remediate the degraded postgres volume vol-0a3f with the storage/infrastructure team; engage the cloud provider if the volume is faulty, and plan failover or migration of the database to healthy storage (logpat-postgres-d629c24d).
Pause or reschedule the report_rollup() workload until storage is healthy, to reduce I/O and connection contention on the already-degraded volume (logpat-postgres-44883ca5).
Keep payment-service 5.8.0 deployed unless storage remediation fails; do not roll back on the basis of this incident, since H2 is rejected (dep-31448d11).

Monitor and, if needed, temporarily raise or tune the 2000ms statement timeout and connection pool limits to reduce user-facing errors while storage is remediated; treat this as a mitigation, not a fix.
preventive_actions: Add alerting on block-device write latency and disk_io_wait for database volumes, so degradation is detected before it reaches checkpoints and query latency (met-postgres-disk_io_wait_ms-1110-1205).
Establish capacity and I/O isolation for reporting workloads (for example, a read replica or off-peak scheduling) so batch jobs cannot amplify contention on the primary.
Add postgres checkpoint-duration and WAL-write-latency alerts to catch slow-checkpoint conditions early (logpat-postgres-7ce84fae).
Review the 835 ms average write latency figure, which rests on a single WARN line, by confirming it with direct volume metrics to strengthen future root-cause evidence.
monitoring_recommendations: Alert when postgres disk_io_wait_ms exceeds a threshold (for example, 20 ms sustained over 5 minutes, baseline is about 2 ms) and when p95_latency_ms rises more than 5x baseline.
Alert on postgres db_conn_util_pct above 80% sustained for 5 minutes, and on any 'checkpoint took' or 'WAL write slow' log lines.
Alert on payment-service and order-service statement-timeout error logs (charges.insert, orders.update) and on payment error_rate above 1%, which is above the 0.8% baseline.
Track the vol-0a3f write-latency WARN message and alert on any occurrence, so storage issues are visible at the first WARN (11:21Z in this incident).
Record deployment events and their start times alongside error-rate panels, so release-timing questions can be answered quickly from dashboards.
limitations: The 835 ms average write latency comes from a single WARN line; the magnitude of the storage effect relies on it and on the disk_io_wait metric.
It is not verified whether the storage degradation is independent of database load.
The contribution of report_rollup() to timeout severity is not quantified.
Autovacuum on public.orders (11:16Z and 11:23Z) may add some I/O load; its effect is judged minor but not measured.
Confidence values are rule-based evidence-strength scores, not calibrated probabilities.
Investigation terminated because: critic verdict APPROVED
conclusion: The most probable root cause of INC-005 is storage degradation on postgres volume vol-0a3f, which slowed database writes and checkpoints and led to statement timeouts and payment and order errors. The evidence from independent sources (postgres logs, disk, latency and connection metrics, and application logs) agrees on this sequence, with the storage warning preceding all user-facing impact by about seven minutes. The payment-service 5.8.0 release and the report_rollup() workload are rejected as root causes, though the rollup may have aggravated contention. Mitigation should focus on the storage volume and on pausing non-essential heavy workloads, with alerting added to catch early storage degradation.
